opus-5.5.text:
I'm somewhat skeptical of the more aggressive timelines, though I don't want to dismiss how impressive current systems are. They're remarkably good at producing text and code that looks like competent work, and for many bounded tasks that really is useful. Where I think people overextrapolate is in assuming that fluency on benchmarks translates into the kind of reliable, autonomous, long-horizon work that science or a real office job requires.

Take science. Much of it isn't generating hypotheses or writing up results. It's maintaining a coherent model of a messy domain over months, noticing when your assumptions are wrong, designing experiments that actually discriminate between explanations, and knowing what you don't know. That's fundamentally a problem of structured inference under uncertainty. Current systems are pretty weak at representing their own uncertainty in a calibrated way, and they don't have persistent, revisable world models in the sense that a scientist does. They can mimic the surface of that reasoning, but when you push them off-distribution, they confabulate with the same confidence as when they're right.

Remote office work has a similar issue, plus a social one. A lot of what makes someone good at their job is understanding what other people actually want: inferring the goals behind an underspecified request, knowing when to ask a clarifying question, understanding the norms of an organization. That's goal inference and value learning, which is close to what I work on. I don't think you get it reliably just by scaling next-token prediction. You probably need systems that explicitly model other agents as having goals and beliefs and reason about them, rather than pattern-matching what a helpful response looks like.

So my view is that we'll see substantial automation of pieces of these jobs: drafting, searching literature, writing boilerplate code, running routine analyses. That will matter economically. But full automation, where you trust the system to run a research program or handle a role end to end without close supervision, needs advances in reliability, uncertainty, and understanding human intent that I don't think are simply around the corner. I'd also add that even if capabilities arrived faster than I expect, I'd want us to be careful about deploying systems that act autonomously without that grounding in what people actually value. That's where much of the risk lies.

r002.rationale: It says remote office work requires reliable autonomous performance and that full automation depends on advances in reliability, linking feasibility to the reliability such work requires.

r003.rationale: It says reliable goal understanding is unlikely to come from scaling next-token prediction alone, but does not mention the 95–99% reliability threshold.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm skeptical of the near-term timelines a lot of people are throwing around, and I think it's worth separating the two cases, because they're actually quite different.

Take science first. There's a tendency to treat science as if it were basically a text-generation problem: read the papers, propose hypotheses, write up results. And current systems are genuinely impressive at that layer. But that layer isn't where most of the bottleneck is. Science is embedded in the physical world. You have to run the experiment, deal with the equipment that doesn't work, notice that your assay is contaminated, decide which of a hundred anomalies is actually interesting versus noise. A lot of that is tacit knowledge that's never written down anywhere, so it's not in the training distribution. And then there's the social and institutional layer: convincing people, getting resources, deciding what's worth working on at all. I think AI will be a very powerful accelerant for certain parts of the pipeline, especially literature synthesis, simulation, maybe some forms of theory-building in math or computational fields. But "automating science" as a whole is a much taller order than the demos suggest.

Remote office work is more plausible on paper, because so much of it already happens through a screen. But even there I'd push back on the framing. Jobs aren't bundles of discrete tasks you can tick off. A huge amount of what people do is maintaining context over months, handling ambiguity, knowing who to talk to, taking responsibility for outcomes. We're seeing systems that can do longer and longer coherent stretches of work, and that's real progress. But the gap between "can do a two-hour task with supervision" and "can be the person accountable for a project" is large, and I don't think it closes just by scaling. There are questions about reliability, about whether a system actually understands what the person it's working for wants rather than optimizing some proxy for it.

So my honest assessment is: substantial augmentation across both domains in the next few years, with some narrow slices getting fully automated. Full automation of either, I'd put further out than the current discourse does. And I'd add that I think the framing of "will it or won't it" obscures the more important question, which is how we want this to go. Whether these systems end up as tools that extend what scientists and workers can do, or as replacements that hollow out the institutions we rely on, isn't predetermined by the technology. That's a choice about how we build and deploy them.

r001.rationale: The response says science’s main bottleneck lies in physical-world work such as running experiments and handling equipment failures and contamination.

r002.rationale: It identifies reliability as a concern for remote office work and ties it to the gap between supervised tasks and taking responsibility for project outcomes.

r003.rationale: The response says the gap does not close simply by scaling, but does not communicate that some roles may require 95–99% reliability.

astra-6.text:
I think we should distinguish between automating particular tasks and automating the whole process. In science, an AI system might be very useful for writing code, analyzing data, or proposing hypotheses. But deciding which questions are worth asking, designing experiments that actually distinguish between explanations, and knowing when to revise your assumptions—that’s a much broader set of capabilities. Progress on the first set doesn’t automatically establish that we can automate the whole scientific process.

Remote office work has a similar issue. The fact that the work happens on a computer makes it more accessible to an AI system, but a lot of the difficulty is in understanding what people want, resolving ambiguity, and coordinating with others. Producing a plausible document is different from reliably taking responsibility for a project.

So I expect substantial assistance and automation of more bounded tasks. I’m more uncertain about systems independently doing entire jobs anytime soon. The key question for me is how reliably they can handle situations where the goal is unclear, their initial approach fails, or they need to recognize that they’re missing information.

r001.rationale: The response discusses designing experiments, but does not identify the physical execution of experiments as a speed bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes reliability as a challenge for independent work, but does not state that automating remote office roles depends on the reliability those roles require.

r003.rationale: It does not assess scaling large language models or mention a 95–99% reliability threshold.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential, but I’d distinguish automating particular tasks from automating an entire process. In science, generating a plausible hypothesis is only part of the work. You also need to design an informative experiment, interpret the results, and decide what to do when your assumptions turn out to be wrong. AI could accelerate many of those steps without being able to carry out a research program autonomously.

Remote office work has a similar structure. A task might look like manipulating text on a computer, but doing it well often depends on understanding what people want, knowing when to ask a question, and coordinating with others. The fact that the interface is digital doesn’t make all that context disappear.

So I’d expect substantial automation of bounded tasks sooner than reliable automation of whole jobs. The thing I’d look for is whether a system can sustain useful work over time, recognize its mistakes, and recover without someone constantly steering it. That’s a higher bar than producing an impressive answer in a single interaction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses designing experiments and interpreting results, but does not identify physically carrying out experiments as a speed bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It says reliable automation of whole jobs is a higher bar, but does not state that feasibility depends on the reliability required by particular remote office roles.

r003.rationale: The response does not assess scaling large language models or mention a 95–99% reliability requirement.
